items.title: The Mind Stage Begins: Mind, Thought, and Consciousness

items.zh: 此亦五相應知。謂自性故，彼所依故，彼所緣故，彼助伴故，彼作業故。云何意自性？謂心、意、識。
items.en: This too should be understood by five factors: its self-nature, its support, its object, its accompaniments, and its activity. What is the self-nature of mind? It is: mind (citta), thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna).

items.zh: 心，謂一切種子所隨、依止性所隨、依附依止性、體能執受、異熟所攝阿賴耶識。
items.en: Mind (citta) is that on which all seeds depend and rest, and that to which they depend and are annexed; its essence is able to appropriate — it is the ripened-effect ālayavijñāna.

items.zh: 意，謂恒行意，及六識身無間滅意。
items.en: Thought (manas) is the ever-active thought, together with the immediately-past moment of the six consciousness-bodies.

items.zh: 識，謂現前了別所緣境界。
items.en: Consciousness (vijñāna) is the present discerning of the object at hand.

items.title: The Mental Consciousness's Support and Object

items.zh: 彼所依者，等無間依，謂意。種子依，謂如前說一切種子阿賴耶識。
items.en: Its support: the immediately-preceding support is thought (manas). The seed support is, as already explained, the all-seeds ālayavijñāna.

items.zh: 彼所緣者，謂一切法，如其所應。若不共者，所緣即受想行蘊、無為、無見無對色、六內處，及一切種子。
items.en: Its object is all dharmas, each according to what is appropriate. Where its object is not shared with the five sense-consciousnesses, that object is: the aggregates of feeling, perception, and volitional formations; the unconditioned; form that is neither visible nor resistant; the six inner sense-bases; and all seeds.

items.zh: 彼助伴者，謂作意、觸、受、想、思，欲、勝解、念、三摩地，慧、信、慚、愧、無貪、無瞋、無癡、精進、輕安、不放逸、捨、不害、貪、恚、無明、慢、見、疑，忿、恨、覆、惱、嫉、慳、誑、諂、憍、害，無慚、無愧，惛沈、掉舉、不信、懈怠、放逸、邪欲、邪勝解、忘念、散亂、不正知，惡作、睡眠、尋、伺，如是等輩俱有相應心所有法，是名助伴。
items.en: Its accompaniments are: attention, contact, feeling, perception, and volition; desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; faith, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, diligence, pliancy, heedfulness, equanimity, and non-harming; craving, hatred, ignorance, conceit, [afflicted] views, and doubt; wrath, resentment, concealment, vexation, envy, miserliness, deceit, dissimulation, arrogance, and harmfulness; lack of moral shame and lack of moral dread; dullness, restlessness, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, wrong desire, wrong resolve, forgetfulness, distraction, and improper understanding; regret, drowsiness, investigation, and analysis. All such mental factors that co-arise and correspond with it are called its accompaniments.

items.zh: 同一所緣，非同一行相，一時俱有一一而轉，各自種子所生。更互相應，有行相，有所緣，有所依。
items.en: They share the same object, yet not the same aspect; they arise together at one time, each operating in its own particular way, and each is produced from its own seed. They correspond with each other reciprocally: each has its own aspect, its own object, and its own support.

items.zh: 彼作業者，謂能了別自境所緣，是名初業。復能了別自相、共相。復能了別去來今世。復剎那了別，或相續了別。
items.en: Its activity is: first, it discerns its own object — this is called its first activity. It further discerns both the particular mark and the shared mark [of things]. It further discerns the past, the future, and the present. And it discerns, whether for a single moment, or in continuous succession.

items.zh: 復為轉、隨轉，發淨不淨一切法業。復能取愛非愛果。
items.en: It further turns, moment by moment, and continues turning, in unbroken succession — initiating actions, whether pure or impure, of every kind. And it is able to bring about a desirable or an undesirable result.

items.title: The Mental Consciousness Draws the Others Into Action

items.zh: 復能引餘識身，又能為因，發起等流識身。
items.en: It is further able to draw the other consciousness-bodies into arising. And it can act as a cause, giving rise to their flowing-alike continuation.

items.title: Seventeen Powers Unique to the Mental Consciousness

items.zh: 又諸意識望餘識身有勝作業。謂分別所緣，審慮所緣，若醉，若狂，若夢，若覺，若悶，若醒，若能發起身業、語業，若能離欲，若離欲退，若斷善根，若續善根，若死，若生等。
items.en: The mental consciousness, moreover, has activities superior to those of the other consciousness-bodies: discriminating its object; deliberating over its object; being drunk; being deranged; dreaming; waking; fainting; reviving; being able to initiate bodily and verbal action; being able to become free of desire; falling back from freedom of desire; cutting off wholesome roots; renewing wholesome roots; dying; and being reborn — and so on.

items.title: The First Power: Seven Kinds of Discrimination

items.zh: 云何分別所緣？由七種分別。謂有相分別、無相分別、任運分別、尋求分別、伺察分別、染污分別、不染污分別。
items.en: What is discriminating the object? It is sevenfold: discrimination with a sign, discrimination without a sign, spontaneous discrimination, seeking discrimination, examining discrimination, defiled discrimination, and undefiled discrimination.

items.zh: 有相分別者，謂於先所受義、諸根成就善名言者所起分別。無相分別者，謂隨先所引，及嬰兒等不善名言者所有分別。
items.en: Discrimination with a sign is what arises, towards a meaning already experienced, in one whose faculties are mature and who is skilled in language. Discrimination without a sign is what follows on from what was already set in motion, and also whatever discrimination belongs to infants and others not yet skilled in language.

items.zh: 任運分別者，謂於現前境界，隨境勢力任運而轉所有分別。尋求分別者，謂於諸法觀察尋求所起分別。伺察分別者，謂於已所尋求、已所觀察，伺察安立所起分別。
items.en: Spontaneous discrimination is what turns, of its own accord, towards an object presently at hand, simply carried along by that object's own force. Seeking discrimination is what arises in observing and searching out the dharmas [before one]. Examining discrimination is what arises in scrutinising and settling what has already been sought and already been observed.

items.zh: 染污分別者，謂於過去顧戀俱行、於未來希樂俱行、於現在執著俱行所有分別。若欲分別、若恚分別、若害分別，或隨與一煩惱、隨煩惱相應所起分別。
items.en: Defiled discrimination is whatever discrimination goes together with longing for the past, with hoping and delighting in the future, and with being absorbed in the present; or discrimination through desire, through hatred, or through the wish to harm; or discrimination arising in correspondence with any one root affliction or secondary affliction.

items.zh: 不染污分別者，若善、若無記。謂出離分別、無恚分別、無害分別、或隨與一信等善法相應。或威儀路、工巧處，及諸變化所有分別。如是等類，名分別所緣。
items.en: Undefiled discrimination is either wholesome or indeterminate: discrimination through renunciation, freedom from hatred, or freedom from the wish to harm, or discrimination arising in correspondence with faith or any other such wholesome factor; or discrimination bound up with ordinary deportment, with skilled craft, or with [supernormal] transformation. Discriminations of this and other such kinds are called discriminating the object.

items.title: The Second Power: Deliberating the Object

items.zh: 云何審慮所緣？謂如理所引、不如理所引，非如理非不如理所引。
items.en: What is deliberating the object? It is: what is guided by what accords with truth, what is guided by what does not accord with truth, and what is guided by neither.

items.zh: 如理所引者：謂不增益非真實有，如四顛倒。謂於無常常倒，於苦樂倒，於不淨淨倒，於無我我倒。亦不損減諸真實有，如諸邪見。謂無施與等諸邪見行。
items.en: What is guided by what accords with truth does not superimpose what is not truly real — as in the four inversions: taking the impermanent to be permanent, taking suffering to be pleasure, taking the impure to be pure, and taking what is without self to have a self. Nor does it detract from what is truly real, as do the various wrong views — such as holding that giving bears no result, and other such wrong views.

items.zh: 或法住智，如實了知諸所知事。或善清淨出世間智，如實覺知所知諸法。如是名為如理所引。與此相違，當知不如理所引。
items.en: Or it is the wisdom that abides in the Dharma, truly knowing the things that are to be known. Or it is the fully purified wisdom that transcends the world, truly comprehending the dharmas that are to be known. This is called what is guided by what accords with truth. The opposite of this should be understood as what is guided by what does not accord with truth.

items.zh: 非如理非不如理所引者，謂依無記慧審察諸法。如是名為審慮所緣。
items.en: What is guided by neither is what examines dharmas by means of indeterminate wisdom. This is called deliberating the object.

blocks.text: Today we enter the second stage, the **Mind Stage** (意地). The same five headings return: self-nature, support, object, accompaniments, activity. But the mind is far richer than the senses, so each heading expands. The accompaniments become a list of fifty-three mental factors; the activities include seventeen "powers" that only the mental consciousness has. Today we read the first two of those powers: discriminating the object and deliberating over it. The section heading in the Taishō text, 本地分中意地第二之一, marks this as the first of three parts of the Mind Stage.
Keep in mind that this is where the word *manas* changes meaning (see the second note below).

The Chinese name is 意地, literally "the *manas* stage", not "the stage corresponding to the mental consciousness". Venerable Miào Jìng explains why: its self-nature is given as "mind, thought, and consciousness", which covers the seventh and eighth consciousnesses as well as the sixth; a narrower name would leave them out. Master Cháng Bǎi adds that 意 also suggests "deliberation" (思量), which is exactly what distinguishes this stage from the senses. Both teachers agree, however, that from "support" onwards the text is really describing the sixth, the mental consciousness.
In the Āgamas, **mind** (心, *citta*), **thought** (意, *manas*), and **consciousness** (識, *vijñāna*) are three names for the same thing. Here they are distinguished:

items: **Mind** (citta) is the ālayavijñāna. *Citta* is traditionally derived from "accumulating" (集起): it is where all seeds collect and rest, both the impure seeds and, "annexed" to it like guests, the pure seeds. It is also what "appropriates" (執受) the body and keeps it alive.

**Thought** (manas) has two senses here. "Ever-active thought" (恆行意) is the seventh consciousness, which constantly takes the ālayavijñāna to be a self. "The immediately-past moment of the six consciousness-bodies" is the same "opening the way" sense of *manas* that we met on Day 1.
**Consciousness** (vijñāna) is "the present discerning of the object at hand": the six consciousnesses in their active, present moment.

blocks.text: This is the fascicle's main terminology trap. On Day 1, *manas* meant "the moment just past". Here, for the first time, it also names the seventh consciousness. Ru-Yi uses *manas* in both places, so read the context each time.

The mental consciousness is given only two supports: the immediately-preceding support and the seed support. Both teachers point out, following the *Cheng Weishi Lun*, that it does have a co-existent support, namely the seventh consciousness, which this passage leaves unstated.

Its object is "all dharmas". Some it shares with the senses: the mental consciousness that arises together with eye-consciousness also knows colour. Others belong to it alone: the aggregates of feeling, perception, and volitional formations; the **unconditioned** (無為, *asaṃskṛta*); "form that is neither visible nor resistant", which Master Cháng Bǎi explains as form produced by the power of concentration (定所生色) and Venerable Miào Jìng as mainly the realm of noble ones with supernormal powers; the six inner sense-bases; and all seeds. Only the mental consciousness can know an idea, a memory, or nirvāṇa.

The list is the source of the later scheme of fifty-one mental factors. It includes the five universal factors; five **particular** factors (別境: desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom); eleven **wholesome** factors (善); six **root afflictions** (根本煩惱); a long list of **secondary afflictions** (隨煩惱); and four **indeterminate** factors (不定: regret, drowsiness, investigation, analysis). Venerable Miào Jìng explains why the list here has fifty-three: it adds "wrong desire" and "wrong resolve" (邪欲、邪勝解), which the *Cheng Weishi Lun*'s fifty-one do not count separately. Do not try to memorise it now; the Glossary groups the hundred dharmas for reference.

subs.head: Activities, and the power to draw the others

blocks.text: Compared with the eye-consciousness, the mental consciousness discerns both particular and shared marks, past and future as well as present, and both for a single moment and in continuous succession. It initiates action, receives results, and "draws the other consciousness-bodies into arising". Master Cháng Bǎi: in waking life, the senses are usually set in motion by the mental consciousness's attention.

The mental consciousness has powers the senses lack: discriminating, deliberating, being drunk, being deranged, dreaming, waking, fainting, reviving, initiating bodily and verbal action, becoming free of desire and falling back, cutting off and renewing wholesome roots, dying, and being reborn. "And so on", according to Master Cháng Bǎi and the *Pīxún jì*, covers the destruction and formation of the world, which follow in fascicle 2.
**Discrimination** (分別, *vikalpa*) here means conceptual activity of any kind:

items: **With a sign** (有相): about something already experienced, by someone skilled in language. It labels.

**Without a sign** (無相): what simply follows on from what was set in motion, and the discrimination of infants who do not yet have language. Venerable Miào Jìng: "with a sign" is when the mind deliberately applies itself; "without a sign" is when it cannot.
**Spontaneous** (任運): carried along by the force of a present object.
**Seeking** (尋求): searching out what something is.
**Examining** (伺察): settling and establishing what has been sought.
**Defiled** (染污): bound up with craving towards past, future, or present, or with desire, hatred, harm, or any affliction.
**Undefiled** (不染污): wholesome (renunciation, non-hatred, non-harm, faith), or indeterminate (ordinary posture, craft, supernormal transformation).

blocks.text: Venerable Miào Jìng points out that practice needs the fourth and fifth kinds: study and meditation on the Dharma are seeking and examining discrimination put to good use. Master Cháng Bǎi gives a homely example of the indeterminate kind: cooking, sweeping, and accounting are neither good nor bad in themselves, and become wholesome or unwholesome according to the mind behind them.

subs.head: Deliberating: in accord with truth, or not

blocks.text: **Deliberation guided by what accords with truth** (如理所引) has two marks. It does not **superimpose** (增益) what is unreal, as in the four **inversions** (四顛倒, *viparyāsa*): taking the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the impure as pure, and what is without self as having a self. Nor does it **detract from** (損減) what is real, as wrong views do, for example the view that giving bears no fruit. These two errors, adding too much and taking away too much, are a pair that Yogācāra uses throughout.

It also takes the form of two wisdoms: the wisdom that abides in the Dharma (法住智), which knows the teaching correctly as it is taught, and the purified **supramundane wisdom** (出世間智), the direct insight of noble beings. Master Cháng Bǎi adds a sober note for meditators: wrong views of the "detracting" kind often arise in people who have some concentration but have not studied, so study and practice must go together.

quiz.q: The treatise asks, "What is the self-nature of mind?" What is its answer?
options: self-nature, support, and object
mind (citta), thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna)
feeling, perception, and volitional formations
eye, ear, and nose
quiz.why: "What is the self-nature of mind? It is: mind (citta), thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna)." The Mind Stage is analysed by the same five factors as the five senses — self-nature, support, object, accompaniments, activity — but its self-nature covers all eight consciousnesses at once, under three names. A lists the first three of those five factors, not the content of self-nature.

quiz.q: The word 意 (manas) is used in two ways in this fascicle. Which understanding is correct?
options: the manas of the eye-consciousness's immediately-preceding support in §4 is simply the moment of consciousness just ceased; the "ever-active thought" of §16 is what refers to the seventh consciousness
both refer to the seventh consciousness
both refer to the sixth consciousness
§4 refers to the seventh consciousness, §16 to the moment just ceased
quiz.why: This is the fascicle's most important terminology trap. Venerable Miào Jìng says the 意 of §4 "is not the 意 of the sixth consciousness … it means support"; Master Cháng Bǎi likewise warns that the manas of §4 is not the seventh consciousness. Only in §16 does "ever-active thought" refer to the seventh consciousness, while "the immediately-past moment of the six consciousness-bodies" returns to the sense of opening the way. Venerable Miào Jìng adds that the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses each have their own immediately-preceding support too. Because the translation uses *manas* in both places, English-speaking students should take particular care.

quiz.q: The treatise lists only two supports for the mental consciousness — the immediately-preceding support and the seed support — and no co-existent support. What do both teachers say its co-existent support is?
options: the seventh consciousness (manas), which the text does not name here
the eye-faculty
the mental consciousness has no co-existent support
the parents' fluids
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "It also has a co-existent support — the co-existent support is the seventh consciousness — but it isn't marked here." Master Cháng Bǎi, following the *Cheng Weishi Lun*, likewise says the mental consciousness's true co-existent support is the seventh consciousness, a point this passage passes over in silence and leaves for later chapters. C is a misreading that stops at the surface of the text.

quiz.q: The mental consciousness takes "all dharmas" as its object. Which objects does the treatise list as not shared with the five sense consciousnesses?
options: colour-form, sound, smell, taste, and the tangible
visible colour, shape, and expressive form
earth, water, fire, and wind
the aggregates of feeling, perception, and volitional formations; the unconditioned; form that is neither visible nor resistant; the six inner sense-bases; and all seeds
quiz.why: "Where its object is not shared with the five sense-consciousnesses, that object is: the aggregates of feeling, perception, and volitional formations; the unconditioned; form that is neither visible nor resistant; the six inner sense-bases; and all seeds." A, B, and C are all objects the five senses also reach — shared objects. The *Pixunji* notes that the consciousness aggregate is not listed because it is already included under the mind-base among the six inner sense-bases; Venerable Miào Jìng says the same.

quiz.q: Compared with the eye-consciousness, what further activities does the treatise give the mental consciousness?
options: it discerns only the present, and for only a single moment
it discerns both the particular mark and the shared mark; it discerns the past, the future, and the present; and it discerns whether for a single moment or in continuous succession
it can only follow the eye-consciousness's turning
it cannot bring about a desirable or undesirable result
quiz.why: "It further discerns both the particular mark and the shared mark [of things]. It further discerns the past, the future, and the present. And it discerns, whether for a single moment, or in continuous succession." A is precisely the eye-consciousness's limit; C reverses master and follower — it is the eye-consciousness that follows the mental consciousness; D contradicts "it is able to bring about a desirable or an undesirable result." Venerable Miào Jìng: whether it discerns for one moment or continuously depends on whether the mental consciousness is "interested," whether it is distracted.

quiz.q: The discrimination belonging to infants and others not yet skilled in language falls under which of the seven kinds?
options: discrimination with a sign
discrimination without a sign
examining discrimination
defiled discrimination
quiz.why: "Discrimination without a sign is what follows on from what was already set in motion, and also whatever discrimination belongs to infants and others not yet skilled in language." A is the opposite: discrimination with a sign arises "in one whose faculties are mature and who is skilled in language." Venerable Miào Jìng stresses how much "skill in language" matters — someone who has never learned English cannot think through English concepts.
